title: What benefit does debt provide a business?
subtitle: The tax shield and financial leverage
openingQuestion: Interest expense of 100 million, tax rate 20%. What is the real tax saved?
openingOptions: 20 million - interest is deducted before tax
explanation: The largest and most measurable benefit of debt is the tax shield: interest is deducted before tax is calculated, so every unit of interest paid reduces the tax owed by exactly the tax rate. As a result, the real cost of debt is lower than the rate stated on the contract. Debt has another, less-discussed benefit: the fixed obligation to pay interest forces management to be disciplined with cash flow, rather than spending it on poorly performing projects.

diagram.label: Reduces the real cost of debt

realWorldExample.company: Capital structure of real estate corporations
realWorldExample.description: Many Vietnamese real estate corporations make full use of the tax shield from bond interest to fund project development - substantially reducing the real cost of capital compared to funding entirely with equity, though it comes with higher financial risk when the market turns difficult.

quiz.question: If the interest rate is 8% and the tax rate is 20%, what is the after-tax cost of debt?
options: 1.6% = 8% × 20% (the tax saved)
10% = 8% ÷ (1 − 20%), dividing instead of multiplying
8% - tax doesn't affect the cost of debt
6.4% = 8% × (1 − 20%), after the tax shield
quiz.explanation: After-tax cost of debt = Kd × (1 − T) = 8% × 0.8 = 6.4%. This is the real cost because interest is tax-deductible. This is why WACC uses the after-tax cost of debt.

quiz.question: If the government raises the corporate tax rate from 20% to 25%, how does the value of the debt tax shield change?
options: Increases - Tax Shield = Interest × Tax rate, higher tax means more saved
No effect at all on the value of a loan's tax shield
Only matters if the company is losing money and doesn't pay tax
Decreases, because a higher tax rate makes the debt's real cost more expensive
quiz.explanation: The formula Tax Shield = Interest Expense × Tax Rate shows a direct relationship: the higher the tax rate, the larger the tax saving from each unit of interest paid - this is why in countries with high corporate tax rates, businesses tend to use more debt.

quiz.question: Interest expense of 100 million, tax rate 20%. What is the tax shield?
options: 80 million (= 100 × 80%, mistaking the after-tax remainder for the tax saved)
20 million (= 100 × 20%, the tax saved)
100 million (the entire interest expense is refunded)
quiz.explanation: Tax Shield = Interest × Tax rate = 100 × 20% = 20 million. This is the tax the business doesn't have to pay because interest is deducted before taxable income is calculated.

quiz.question: Why doesn't the tax shield turn debt into a free source of capital?
options: Because the tax shield only applies to loans with terms over five years
Because tax authorities cap the amount of interest deductible each year
Because the business still has to pay the remaining interest in real cash
Because the bank charges an arrangement fee that offsets the savings
quiz.explanation: Borrowing 100 million at 8% means paying 8 million, of which the government effectively covers 1.6 million, but the business still pays 6.4 million in real cash. The tax shield makes debt cheaper, not free.

quiz.question: A business is losing money and doesn't pay tax. What happens to its tax shield?
options: It converts into a receivable from the tax authority next year
It stays the same because interest is always recorded as an expense
It simply carries forward untouched
It has no effect because there's no tax to deduct against
quiz.explanation: With no taxable income, there's nothing to shield. The paradox is that the weakest business - where debt is most dangerous - is exactly where the benefit of debt disappears.

keyTakeaways: Debt is cheaper than equity after adjusting for tax

practicePrompt.question: A company borrows 1,000 billion at an interest rate of 8%/year (interest expense = 80 billion/year), with a corporate tax rate of 20%. How much 'tax shield' does the company save each year thanks to this loan?
options: Tax shield = Interest × Tax rate = 80 × 0.2 = 16 billion/year - this is the tax the company saves because interest is deductible before calculating corporate income tax
Tax shield = 1,000 × 0.2 = 200 billion, calculated on the total loan rather than the interest
Tax shield = 80 billion, equal to the entire interest expense payable each year
The tax shield doesn't exist because the company still has to pay the full 80 billion in interest every year regardless
practicePrompt.explanation: Tax shield = Interest × Tax rate = 80 × 0.2 = 16 billion/year. This is the tax benefit the company enjoys because interest is an expense deductible before calculating corporate income tax - one of the reasons debt can create value for a company (though it comes with higher financial risk).

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Calculate a tax shield yourself
application.message: Take a company's interest expense from its financial statements, multiply by the corporate tax rate to get the real tax shield the company enjoys that year.
application.secondary: This figure explains part of why many companies choose to use debt instead of equity.

sections.text: Debt is often seen as a burden, but in Corporate Finance it has a concrete, measurable benefit: the tax shield - the tax saved because interest is deductible before corporate income tax is calculated.

When a business takes on debt, interest is recorded as an expense and deducted before calculating taxable profit. **Example:** interest expense of 100 million, tax rate 20% → Tax Shield = 100 million × 20% = 20 million VND of tax saved. So the real cost of debt is always lower than the stated interest rate: After-tax cost of debt = Interest rate × (1 − Tax rate). If the borrowing rate is 8% and the tax rate is 20%, the real cost is only 8% × 0.8 = 6.4%.
The higher the tax rate, the more attractive debt becomes

Because Tax Shield = Interest × Tax rate, the relationship between the two is direct: the higher the corporate tax rate, the more tax each unit of interest saves. This is why in countries with high corporate tax rates, businesses tend to use more debt leverage to optimize their tax burden - and it's also why many Vietnamese real estate corporations make use of corporate bonds to both raise capital and enjoy the tax shield, though this comes with higher financial risk when the market turns difficult.

items: Tax shield = Interest expense × Corporate tax rate
After-tax cost of debt = Interest rate × (1 − Tax rate)
This is why WACC always uses the after-tax cost of debt, not the stated rate
The tax benefit only has value if the business has profit to deduct against - a loss-making company doesn't enjoy the tax shield

lines: Debt is cheaper than equity after adjusting for tax - but cheaper doesn't mean safer.
